title: Grandma’s Mint Jelly
source: From Grandma  ·  Easter, spring dinners, and Sunday roasts
occasionText: Easter, spring dinners, and Sunday roasts
headnote: A staple in Grandma’s refrigerator, and always on the table when there was lamb.

items.raw: 1½ packed cups (45 g) fresh mint leaves, plus 2 tablespoons finely chopped
½ teaspoon mint flavoring, if it needs more flavor
4 half-pint jars with new lids and bands

steps.text: Bruise the 1½ cups of mint leaves by crushing them in your hands or with a rolling pin. Bring the water to a boil, pour it over the leaves in a heatproof bowl, cover, and steep 15 minutes. Strain through a fine sieve, pressing on the leaves. Measure 1½ cups of mint liquid, adding water if you are short.
Wash the jars, lids, and bands in hot soapy water. Sterilize the jars in boiling water for 10 minutes and keep them hot until filling — hot jelly in a cold jar can crack it.

In a large, deep saucepan, combine the 1½ cups mint liquid, the lemon juice, vinegar, and sugar. Stir over high heat until the sugar dissolves, then bring to a full rolling boil — a boil that does not stop when you stir it.

Stir in the liquid pectin all at once, with the chopped mint, the mint flavoring if the mint taste is weak, and the coloring if using. Return to a full rolling boil and boil hard for exactly 1 minute, stirring constantly. Remove from the heat and skim off any foam.
Ladle the hot jelly into the hot jars, leaving ¼ inch of headspace. Wipe the rims with a clean damp cloth, center the lids, and screw the bands on firmly.
Turn the sealed jars upside down for 5 minutes, then turn them upright. This is how Linda does it — she does not water-bath them.
Leave the jars undisturbed 24 hours; the jelly can take up to 2 days to fully set. Press the center of each lid — if it pops back, refrigerate that jar and use it first.

notes.label: Linda’s notes
notes.text: she usually adds ½ teaspoon mint flavoring when the jelly needs more flavor, and seals the jars by turning them upside down rather than processing them.

notes.label: Food-safety note
notes.text: turning jars upside down is the old-fashioned method. Current USDA guidance is a 10-minute boiling-water bath (longer above 1,000 feet) for jars kept at room temperature; jars that are not water-bathed are safest kept in the refrigerator.

notes.label: Do not change the ratio
notes.text: liquid pectin sets only with the right balance of sugar and acid. Do not reduce the sugar, and make two batches rather than doubling.

notes.label: Serving
notes.text: serve at room temperature with roast leg of lamb or lamb chops. Spearmint gives the classic flavor.
